column4: God dislikes the hypocrites’ setting out (انْبِعَاثَهُمْ), restrains them, and they are told to sit; this exact cognate reverses the source dictionary scene of a hobbled camel released and made to rise.

The sun may not overtake the moon, nor night outstrip day, and each moves in an orbit; this sets a cosmic boundary around the section’s picture of the moon following the sun like a calf following its dam.
Pilgrims come on every lean mount from distant passes; the journey-worn camel body and sustained gait give a Qur’anic scene for the source’s easy-moving camel.

The verse names a pair of camels and asks whether God forbade the males, the females, or what the females’ wombs contain; it directly joins camel sex, maternal body, and offspring while exposing invented restrictions.
Moses and Aaron are to tell Pharaoh that they are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds; this supplies the r-s-l office whose requested release follows in 26:17.
The messengers command Pharaoh to “send/release with us” the Children of Israel; it repeats the section’s relation between messenger and the act of letting a restrained party go.
Moses identifies himself to Pharaoh as a messenger from the Lord of the worlds, setting up the same r-s-l wordplay completed by release in 7:105.
After presenting clear proof, Moses commands Pharaoh to send/release the Children of Israel with him; the verse makes release the messenger’s concrete demand.

Immediately after the camel’s grazing right, Thamud is reminded that God settled it in the land and is warned not to spread corruption there; its expansive occupation sharpens the wrong of denying one animal room to graze.
Salih reminds Thamud that God produced them from the earth and settled them in it; this frames the later command to let Allah’s camel eat in that same divinely granted earth.
The Thamud passage places the people amid gardens and springs; their abundant water makes resistance to the she-camel’s single allotted drink especially pointed.
Crops and palms heavy with fruit complete the provision surrounding Thamud; this is the edible landscape in which they deny the camel her measured share.
The people of al-Hijr, Thamud’s community, deny the messengers; this is a compact parallel to the denial that precedes violence against the camel.
God gives the people His signs and they turn away from them; in the fuller Thamud accounts the she-camel is precisely such a sign.
They carve mountain houses while feeling secure; the apparently protected dwellings make the morning destruction of the camel’s people a bodily and spatial reversal.
The blast seizes them in the morning, supplying another direct continuation from Thamud’s rejected signs to communal punishment.
What Thamud had acquired does not avail it; the verse closes the al-Hijr account by stripping away the security named around its houses.
Thamud is shown guidance but prefers blindness, so the humiliating thunderbolt seizes it for what it earned; this states the chosen moral movement behind the hand that attacks the camel.
God saves those who believe and are mindful, separating them from the Thamud body seized in 41:17 just as other camel accounts save Salih and his hearers.
Thamud is said to have denied the Striking Calamity; the terse statement joins its denial to the catastrophe specified in 69:5.
Thamud is destroyed by the overwhelming blast, adding a concise formulation of what follows the camel crime even though the animal is not named here.

Human beings allocate what is in livestock wombs to men, forbid it to wives, and share it if stillborn; these invented rules over female animal bodies contrast with God’s explicit apportionment of the she-camel’s right.
Hell’s sparks are compared to yellow camels; the simile turns the familiar mass and motion of camel bodies into fire, an opposite use of the section’s living female animal.
Livestock carry loads to lands people could reach only with severe hardship; this makes the animal’s body and ease of travel the benefit corresponding to the source’s camel of easy gait.

Mothers nurse their children for a complete term, receive provision, and must not be harmed through the child; this human law clarifies the section’s nursing-young detail as a protected relation of body, feeding, and due share.

The brothers ask for an added camel-load; because the source itself glosses b-ʿ-th with بَعِير, the ayah offers a specific but indirect view of the camel body as a unit of carrying capacity rather than a body being raised.
The herald promises a camel-load to whoever recovers the cup; the camel is again an implicit bodily measure of burden, a peripheral counterpart to the source’s بَعِير under release and movement.

The oath by “those sent forth” uses a feminine plural of r-s-l and depicts ordered release or motion, but the referents are disputed; it is therefore only an uncertain lexical echo of the source’s easily dispatched مَرَاسِيل camels.
